item.title: "This document cannot be formatted as intended": Chrome's XSLT message
item.description:
Since Chrome 158, released on 17 November 2026, some pages show this message instead of their usual content:

This document cannot be formatted as intended. It uses XSLT, which the browser does not support. You might be able to install a browser extension that allows you to view it.

Quick answer: nothing is broken on your computer. The page was built with XSLT, an old way of styling XML that Chrome has now removed. The data is still there, only unformatted. To see the page as before, install the free XSLT Polyfill extension and reload. If your company manages Chrome, IT can switch XSLT back on until August 2027 (see below). If the site is yours, test its stylesheet outside the browser: that is the first step of every fix.

item.title: The XSLT Polyfill extension: view XSLT pages in Chrome again
item.description:
Quick answer: XSLT Polyfill is a free browser extension that puts XSLT back for the pages that need it. Install it from the Chrome Web Store, reload the page, and it renders the way it used to. It is the extension Chrome’s own message points to, and the one Chrome’s documentation recommends. There is also a Firefox version.

Why you need it

Since Chrome 158 (17 November 2026), Chrome no longer runs XSLT. Pages built with it show raw XML and a message saying the browser does not support XSLT, and web apps that called XSLTProcessor break. The extension restores both.

item.title: This site uses XSLT: what Chrome's banner means
item.description:
Update, 22 November 2026: Chrome 158 shipped on 17 November and the removal has happened. The banner is gone; affected pages now show raw XML and the message “This document cannot be formatted as intended”. If that is what you are seeing, go to what that message means and how to view the page. The rest of this page is kept for reference.

item.title: Your RSS feed's stylesheet stopped rendering
item.description:
Quick answer: your feed keeps working. Feed readers never used the stylesheet — they parse the XML. What broke on 17 November 2026, with Chrome 158, is only the friendly page a human sees when they click the feed link in a browser: instead of your styled “subscribe to this feed” page, Chrome shows the raw XML tree.

This is the most common way sites run into Chrome’s XSLT removal, and the least damaging.
